title: How to read a developer's track record before you reserve
excerpt: A launch brochure shows intent. A handed-over community shows what the developer actually does. Here is how to check the second before you commit to the first.
content: Judge a developer by what it has already handed over, not by what it has launched. Visit a completed community, read the registered project details, and speak to residents before you reserve.

sections.title: Start with delivered communities, not the launch event
sections.text: Ask for a list of completed projects and visit one on a weekday evening. Notice how the landscaping has matured, whether lifts and car parks are well kept, and how quickly shops and schools opened. A developer's best marketing is a finished neighbourhood that people still want to live in.

sections.title: Compare promised and actual handover
sections.text: Find the original launch announcement for a past project and compare its stated completion window with the real handover. A small slip is normal on large projects; a pattern of long delays is information. Ask the sales team directly how their last three projects performed against schedule.

sections.title: Check the registration and the paper trail
sections.text: In Dubai, off-plan projects should be registered with the Dubai Land Department and carry a project registration number. Ask for it, and confirm on the official channels that your unit and the developer match. If something cannot be checked, treat that as an answer.

sections.title: Talk to owners, not only agents
sections.text: Residents of a past project can tell you things a brochure cannot: how maintenance responds, how service charges have moved, and whether the facilities match the renders. Owner groups and building managers are usually happy to give an honest view.

sections.title: Match the developer to your goal
sections.text: A master-planner with large communities suits buyers who want infrastructure and long-term neighbourhood growth. A design-led boutique developer suits buyers who value architecture and are comfortable with a smaller, riskier track record. Neither is better; they answer different questions.

title: Escrow, Oqood and the off-plan paper trail
excerpt: Three pieces of paperwork protect most off-plan buyers in Dubai. Here is what each one is, what it does, and what to keep.
content: Buyer payments for registered off-plan projects in Dubai are meant to go into the project's escrow account, and the sale is recorded through the interim registration system known as Oqood. Keep every document and pay only into the account named in your contract.

sections.title: The escrow account
sections.text: Dubai's regulations require developers of registered off-plan projects to hold buyer payments in a project-specific escrow account, from which funds are released against construction progress. For you, that means the account details in your contract matter: pay only into the named escrow account, never to a personal or general company account.

sections.title: Oqood: the interim registration
sections.text: Off-plan sale contracts are recorded through an interim register at the Dubai Land Department, commonly called Oqood. It links you, the unit and the project. Ask your adviser to explain what was registered, when, and how to obtain the registration certificate.

sections.title: The sale and purchase agreement
sections.text: The agreement sets out the payment schedule, the handover window, what happens on delay and what you may and may not do before handover. Read the clauses on delay, cancellation and assignment before you sign, and ask for plain-language explanations of anything unclear.

sections.title: What to keep
sections.text: Keep the signed agreement, every payment receipt, the escrow account details, the registration certificate and every written exchange with the developer. If you buy from abroad, scan them into one folder so a family member or lawyer can find them quickly.

sections.title: Where to confirm
sections.text: Rules and procedures change, and individual projects differ. Confirm the current requirements with the Dubai Land Department and the Real Estate Regulatory Agency, or with a licensed adviser, rather than relying on this summary.

title: Dubai, Abu Dhabi or Sharjah: choose the emirate before the project
excerpt: Developers such as Emaar, Aldar and Arada have made it possible to buy in three emirates from one conversation. The decision that matters comes first: which emirate fits your plan.
content: Pick the emirate for your life and your goal first, then the developer and the project. Ownership rules, lifestyle and rental demand differ between Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah.

sections.title: Ownership rules are set emirate by emirate
sections.text: Property ownership for non-citizens depends on the emirate and on designated freehold or investment zones. Before you fall for a project, confirm that it sits in an area where your ownership type is allowed, and ask what that ownership covers.

sections.title: Dubai: depth and choice
sections.text: Dubai offers the largest range of developers, communities and resale activity. It suits buyers who value choice, a deep rental market and the option to sell to a wide pool of buyers later.

sections.title: Abu Dhabi: master communities and calm
sections.text: Aldar's island communities on Saadiyat, Yas and Fahid suit buyers who want a quieter, more planned environment and a capital-city setting. Resale and rental dynamics differ from Dubai, so ask for local evidence rather than assuming the same pattern.

sections.title: Sharjah: a different pace and a different entry point
sections.text: Arada's Aljada and Masaar communities are changing how people look at Sharjah, as a place to live with a cultural core and calmer streets, within commuting distance of Dubai. Check the commute honestly at the times you would travel.

sections.title: Let the daily routine decide
sections.text: List where you will work, where children will go to school and how often you will travel. Then test each emirate against that list. The right project is usually obvious once the emirate is right.

title: Read a payment plan like a cash-flow schedule
excerpt: A payment plan is a timetable of obligations. Turning it into your own cash-flow calendar shows whether it works before you sign.
content: Convert any payment plan into a month-by-month calendar in your own currency, then add the costs the plan does not show. If the calendar looks tight in any single month, ask for a different structure or a different project.

sections.title: Know which type of plan you are looking at
sections.text: Some plans tie instalments to construction milestones; others to fixed dates; some extend after handover. Each moves risk differently. Milestone plans track progress; date plans do not; post-handover plans can ease the burden after you receive keys but extend the commitment.

sections.title: Build the calendar yourself
sections.text: List every instalment with its date or trigger. Add the one-off costs around a purchase, such as registration fees and agency fees, and the recurring ones after handover, such as service charges. Ask your adviser to confirm the current fees rather than assuming.

sections.title: Think in your own currency
sections.text: The dirham is pegged to the US dollar, so exchange-rate risk for buyers paying from India, Pakistan, Russia or the UK sits in your home currency against the dollar. If your income is in rupees, rubles or sterling, test the plan against a weaker home currency.

sections.title: Ask what happens when plans slip
sections.text: Find out how the contract treats a late payment, a handover delay and a request to change the schedule. These clauses matter more than the headline structure.

sections.title: Compare plans on total commitment, not on the first payment
sections.text: A low first payment can hide a heavier tail. Compare plans by the full schedule and by how the final payments line up with your own expected income.

title: Branded residences: what the name adds, and what it cannot
excerpt: From Dorchester Collection on Palm Jumeirah to Mercedes-Benz in Downtown, the UAE has become a market for brand-named homes. Here is how to think about the premium.
content: A brand name can bring design standards and hotel-grade service, but it does not remove the need to read the operating agreement, the service charges and the exit route.

sections.title: What the brand usually brings
sections.text: Hospitality names such as Dorchester Collection, Four Seasons and Anantara typically bring a service model, concierge and design standards. Automotive and fashion names, such as Mercedes-Benz Places, Bugatti Residences and Armani Beach Residences, bring a design language and a community of fans of the marque.

sections.title: What it does not change
sections.text: The building still has to be well built, well managed and well located. The name does not change who the developer is, how the project is financed or how the escrow account works. Judge those the same way as for any other project.

sections.title: Read the operating terms
sections.text: Ask who runs the building, how long the brand licence lasts, what happens if the brand leaves, and how service charges are set. These terms shape both your annual costs and your future resale.

sections.title: Think about the exit
sections.text: A branded home may appeal to a narrower group of future buyers. Ask for evidence of resale activity in comparable branded buildings, and be sceptical of promises about future value.

sections.title: Match the brand to how you will use it
sections.text: If you will live there, the service and design may justify themselves. If you plan to rent it out, ask how the brand's own reputation affects tenant demand, and compare it with a good non-branded building nearby.

title: Questions to ask at the sales gallery, and the answers that should worry you
excerpt: A sales gallery is built to make you feel good. These questions turn the visit into a fact-finding session.
content: Bring a written list. Ask about registration, escrow, delivery history, service charges, and what is and is not included. Note who answers directly and who changes the subject.

sections.title: Is this project registered, and can I see the number?
sections.text: A registered project has a number you can verify. A vague answer, or a promise to send it later, is a signal to slow down and check on the official channels first.

sections.title: Where do my payments go?
sections.text: The answer should be the project's escrow account. If anyone suggests paying elsewhere, stop and speak to your adviser.

sections.title: What did you hand over last, and when did you promise it?
sections.text: Compare the promised and actual dates. Ask to visit the completed project. A confident developer will arrange it.

sections.title: What is not in the model?
sections.text: Show models often include finishes, furniture and views that are not in the standard unit. Ask what is included, what is optional and what will be different in the finished building.

sections.title: What are the running costs?
sections.text: Ask for the expected service charge basis, how it is set and what it covers. A building's charges shape what it feels like to own it for years after the sales gallery is gone.

title: Buying from abroad: a checklist for non-resident buyers
excerpt: Many SWK clients buy from India, Pakistan, Russia and the UK without visiting first. This checklist covers what to line up before you transfer a dirham.
content: Confirm your home-country rules for sending money abroad, line up your identification and source-of-funds paperwork, and appoint someone you trust to attend viewings and handover.

sections.title: Check the rules at home first
sections.text: Many countries regulate how much money residents can send abroad and for what purpose. Check the rules that apply to you, such as India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, with your bank or a qualified adviser before you commit to a payment schedule.

sections.title: Prepare identity and source-of-funds documents
sections.text: Developers, banks and the regulator will ask who you are and where the money comes from. Having passports, proof of address and evidence of funds ready speeds everything up and avoids last-minute surprises.

sections.title: Use the right payment channel
sections.text: Pay by bank transfer to the named escrow account, from an account in your own name where possible. Avoid cash and third-party payers, and keep every transfer receipt.

sections.title: Appoint someone you trust
sections.text: A family member or adviser who can attend viewings, sign for keys and inspect the handover can make remote buying far smoother. If you grant a power of attorney, keep its scope as narrow as it can be.

sections.title: Plan for handover and afterwards
sections.text: Think about who will furnish, let or manage the home, how service charges will be paid, and how you will receive notices. A purchase made from abroad still needs a person on the ground.

title: Off-plan or ready in Dubai? Start with the date you need the keys
excerpt: A practical comparison of cash flow, handover uncertainty and the checks to make before choosing a Dubai property.
content: An off-plan apartment and a ready apartment can share the same price and still ask very different things of your finances. Start with when you need the home, how much cash you can commit and what happens if your timetable changes.

sections.title: Put your own deadline first
sections.text: If you need somewhere to live soon, begin with homes you can inspect and a realistic transfer timetable. A ready property is not necessarily vacant: ask about occupancy, access and the basis on which possession will be delivered. With off-plan, make a separate plan for where you will live until completion. Treat the advertised handover date as a point to investigate in the contract, rather than a moving date you have already secured.

sections.title: Compare payments on a calendar
sections.text: Write down every payment date, including the reservation, construction instalments and any amount due at handover. Alongside it, list the cash you expect to have available at that time. A smaller initial payment can look comfortable while leaving a difficult final instalment. For a ready home, ask for an itemised estimate of transfer and financing costs. Compare both options on the same basis rather than comparing only the deposit.

sections.title: Check the project, then the paperwork
sections.text: Dubai Land Department provides a project-status enquiry through Dubai REST. Its Dubai REST information page describes access to completion information, project photographs and escrow details. Use official project information alongside the documents supplied by the seller or developer. Ask a qualified adviser to explain provisions about delays, cancellation and resale restrictions before committing money.

sections.title: Look at what you can actually inspect
sections.text: A finished home lets you examine light, noise, room dimensions and common areas. Visit at a time that resembles your daily routine. A show apartment can help you understand a proposed layout, but ask which finishes, views and fittings are contractual. Save the agreed specification with the signed documents. For either route, confirm parking, storage and the area measurement used in the listing.

sections.title: Do not spend tomorrow’s rent today
sections.text: A ready home may be available to rent after completion, but vacancy, repairs or an existing tenancy can change the timing and amount. An off-plan home cannot provide occupied rental income before it is delivered and usable. Build a cash reserve around your actual obligations. Price growth and future rent should remain assumptions you can change, not money needed to make the purchase work.

sections.title: Bring a brief that makes the shortlist useful
sections.text: Send your consultant a budget ceiling, preferred areas, bedroom requirement and intended use. Add the latest date by which you need access and the payments you can comfortably make. Ask for one ready option and one off-plan option with their payment timelines side by side. The better choice is the one that fits your constraints after the documents have been checked, not the one with the most persuasive launch brochure.

title: Dubai property Golden Visa: questions to settle before you buy
excerpt: Understand the property route, check mortgage documentation and separate a purchase decision from a residency application.
content: Dubai Land Department lists a property-investor route for a renewable ten-year residence permit with a qualifying purchase value of at least AED 2 million. That threshold is a starting point for an eligibility check, not a promise of approval for a particular purchase.

sections.title: Start with the authority’s current requirements
sections.text: Use the official DLD investor service page as the starting point. It describes the qualifying purchase value and documents for its route. Eligibility depends on your ownership and application circumstances. Before paying a reservation amount, ask the relevant service centre to confirm how the proposed transaction will be treated. Keep the answer with your purchase documents and check it again if the financing or ownership arrangement changes.

sections.title: If there is a mortgage, ask a precise question
sections.text: DLD’s service information specifies a bank letter showing AED 2 million paid for a mortgaged property. Do not assume that a property’s advertised value alone settles the mortgage question. Ask what evidence is required for your particular bank and purchase structure. A broker’s indicative mortgage calculation and an immigration eligibility assessment answer different questions; obtain both where relevant.

sections.title: Choose a home that also works without the visa
sections.text: Think through location, condition, running costs and how long you expect to own the property. Would it still suit your needs if the residency application took longer than expected? If it is intended as a rental investment, test the income assumptions separately. A property purchase creates financial commitments even while an application is being assessed. Leave room in your budget for both the property and the application process.

sections.title: Prepare documents without sending them to strangers
sections.text: Ask the official service channel for its current checklist and submit identity and ownership documents through that channel. Keep names and ownership details consistent across the documents you provide. Avoid sending passport scans or banking information through an open website chat. SWK’s website assistant can help you identify the next conversation; it does not assess documents or issue immigration decisions.

sections.title: Separate official charges from service charges
sections.text: Request a written breakdown that distinguishes government charges, medical or identity-related steps where applicable, and any professional assistance fee. Confirm the current amounts and what is included before instructing a provider. This guide does not quote a fixed all-in price or a guaranteed processing period, because those details need confirmation for the actual application.

sections.title: Questions for your first conversation
sections.text: Explain whether the property is already owned, whether there is financing and whose names appear on the ownership documents. Ask which documents establish qualifying value, what additional steps apply to family members and where the application should be submitted. Confirm the rules with the relevant authority before relying on the purchase for your residency plans. SWK can discuss the property search; the authority determines residency eligibility.

title: Comparing Dubai rental yields: five neighbourhoods, one honest worksheet
excerpt: A practical way to compare JVC, Business Bay, Dubai Marina, Dubai Hills and Dubai South without relying on unsupported yield rankings.
content: There is no single rental yield for an entire Dubai neighbourhood. The purchase price, building costs, condition and rent actually achieved matter more than a headline league table. Compare individual units with the same worksheet before choosing an area.

sections.title: Use one definition of yield
sections.text: For a simple gross yield, divide annual rent by purchase price and multiply by 100. A home priced at AED 1 million with AED 70,000 annual rent has a hypothetical gross yield of 7%. That is an illustration, not an estimate for a current listing. Net income requires a second calculation that deducts your expected operating costs. Financing and acquisition costs should also be shown separately so you can see what the property earns and what cash reaches you.

sections.title: Jumeirah Village Circle: compare the building
sections.text: For a JVC shortlist, compare units with a similar size and layout rather than grouping every apartment under the community name. Ask about service charges, parking, access and the condition of common areas. A lower purchase price can be attractive, but it should be considered with the cost of keeping the apartment ready for the next tenant. Ask what evidence supports the proposed rent for that specific building.

sections.title: Business Bay and Dubai Marina: compare daily use
sections.text: Look beyond proximity to a recognisable skyline. Check the journey from the building entrance to transport, the practical parking arrangement and the noise at the times a resident would be home. In Marina, inspect access and waterfront orientation; in Business Bay, check the exact location and surrounding works. Two apartments described as being in the same area can offer very different everyday experiences. Match your rental comparison to the actual unit.

sections.title: Dubai Hills and Dubai South: compare what is available now
sections.text: When discussing these communities, distinguish existing amenities from future plans and measure the commute yourself. Identify the tenant you expect the home to suit and the features that tenant would use. Ask for comparable units with similar delivery and occupancy status. A future facility or hoped-for rental premium should be an explicit scenario in your worksheet, with a second case that does not rely on it.

sections.title: Build a downside case
sections.text: Repeat the calculation with one month of vacancy, a maintenance allowance and a lower rent assumption. Include furnishing and management costs if they apply to your intended letting arrangement. For financed purchases, add repayments to a cash-flow view without confusing them with gross yield. If an ordinary repair or a delayed tenancy makes the figures unmanageable, revisit the price or the cash reserve before making an offer.

sections.title: Check evidence and its date
sections.text: DLD’s open-data pages provide routes to transaction and rent information, including historical data. Record the date, property type and period used in your comparison. Separate advertised asking rents from evidence of actual agreements, and ask about differences between the comparable and the home you are considering. Bring SWK two or three candidate units with the same cost assumptions. A useful comparison explains uncertainty rather than promising a return.
